Welcome to day two of Medical Lien Balance Verification training. Yesterday set the foundation, and today we get practical. We will walk through how a lien balance verification request is built and sent, how to create and save it in the case management system, the best practices that go with it, the Final Lien Ledger, and how we track every balance so nothing is missed before the case closes.

Here is our outline for today. We start with the Lien Balance Verification Request itself, what goes into it and how it moves. Then we look at creating and saving the LBV, which is our short name for the lien balance verification. After that, CMS navigation and best practices, and we finish with tracking. Keep these four parts in mind, because each one builds on the one before it.

Our first section is the Lien Balance Verification Request. This is the written request we send to a lienholder asking them to confirm exactly what is owed on our client's account. On a settlement team, this number feeds directly into the client's net, so getting it right matters. Let's look at why we do it and then walk the process step by step.

Why do we verify? This essential step protects both the firm and the client from medical expenses that go beyond the established limits. If we pay off a number nobody confirmed, the firm can carry the loss or the liability, and the client's net shrinks. Verifying the balance before settlement closes is how we avoid those surprises during the claim's settlement process.

Step one is gathering the relevant information. You need the client details: full name, claim number, date of birth and case number. You need the lienholder information, meaning who is holding the lien, whether that is an attorney, a health insurer, a medical provider or a hospital. And you need the service details: the dates of service or treatment and the total amount claimed. Missing details slow everything down, so check this list before you draft.

Step two is drafting the Lien Balance Verification request. Keep it formal and concise. The lienholder's billing team should be able to read it quickly and know whose account we are asking about and what we need back. Include the essential information from step one so they can process the verification without having to come back to us with questions.

When you draft, start by preparing the request form for the client's balance. Fill out the necessary fields before it goes anywhere: date of service, account number, fax number, email and phone. And where you have already been in touch with a provider, send a confirmation email that builds on that prior correspondence, so the request connects to the conversation you already had.

Sometimes a provider has sent the account to a collections agency. When that happens, the agency is who you contact about the balance. Ask specifically for the client's balance, and do not settle for a verbal figure. Request an email or fax confirmation that clearly displays the balance, so the file has written proof of what the agency says is owed.

Here is a sample request letter for lien verification. Notice the callouts. Edit the line showing how it is being sent, facsimile, email or both, and make sure the fax number or email address matches. Add your initials beside the attorney's initials in small caps. The response section asks for last day of treatment, whether treatment is complete, total charges, insurance payments, adjustments and the final lien balance, plus a billing statement.

Step three is sending the request. Use whatever method the lienholder prefers, whether that is certified mail, email or fax. Whichever you use, make sure you keep a record that it went out. That record is what lets you follow up with confidence and show exactly when the request was made, for example the fax confirmation sheet or the sent email saved to the file.

Step four is reviewing the lienholder's response. Do not just copy the balance into the file. Review the balance details and make sure every charge is accurate and consistent with what is already documented in our records, such as treatment dates and payments we know about. If something does not match, that is a discrepancy to raise before the number is relied on.

Sometimes a billing representative will verify the balance over the phone. That is helpful, but a phone call is not documentation. Follow up by sending a confirmation letter or email that puts what you were told in writing. That way the file has a record if the number is ever questioned later. Let's look at an example of that confirmation email next.

This is an example of a confirmation email after a phone call. It names the provider, confirms the conversation, states the accident date, the client's name and the balance given, here zero dollars, along with the date of birth. Notice the closing line: if we do not hear otherwise within ten business days, we treat this as the correct and final balance. The boxed fields are what you change each time.

Step five is negotiating if necessary. If the response shows discrepancies, or the lien amount is higher than expected, we engage with the lienholder to resolve the issue or dispute. Sometimes that simply means correcting an error. Other times it means a reduction request, which is covered in the reductions training. Always follow the firm's approval process and get any agreed amount in writing.

Now we move into the case management system, or CMS. This section shows where the request is actually built and saved, using screenshots from Litify and Filevine. Your firm's system may look different, but the steps are the same idea: find the provider, pull the template, fill it in, send it, save it and document what you did.

Step one in the CMS is opening the client's matter and going to the Meds Tab, where the treating providers are listed. Find the provider you are sending the request to, and confirm it is the right entity and location. Picking the wrong provider entry means the request goes to the wrong place or carries the wrong contact details.

This screenshot is from Litify. You can see the Medical Records list for the matter, with each record's number, the date it was created and the provider. The boxed record numbers are what you click to open each provider's record. Before you go further, make sure the record you open matches the provider you are requesting the balance from.

Once you open the provider, extract the contact information of the facility we are verifying with. In this Litify example, the phone number is boxed on the account details. Also watch for banners like the red one at the top, which here gives an updated billing number. Using current contact details means your request reaches the right billing office the first time.

After every call, summarize the conversation and outcome in the case notes within your CMS. In this Litify example, the call log has a subject, a call type, and a comments box, and you save it when done. A good note says who you spoke with and what you learned, so anyone picking up the file later knows exactly where the balance stands.

Step three is selecting the template. Within the Meds Tab, go to the Medical LOR and Lien Balance Verification section. Then open Lien BV for Provider and Lien Holder and select the template called Lien BV v2, Provider and Lien Holder, with the date. Using the current template keeps every letter consistent and makes sure it asks for all the right fields.

Here is what that looks like in Filevine. The Medical LOR and Lien Balance Verification section sits in the Meds tab, and the boxed area on the right is Lien BV for Provider and Lien Holder, where the generated template appears. Remember this is illustrated in Filevine, so the layout may be different in your firm's CMS.

Step four is downloading the file. Use the dropdown arrow to the right of the document, or open the file and click the download button in the upper right corner of the pop-up page. Either way works. The point is to get the generated letter onto your computer so you can complete it.

This screenshot shows the dropdown arrow next to the Lien BV v2 document. Open the menu and hit Download to start the download. The other options, like preview, rename and move, are there too, but for now all you need is the download. Again, this is Filevine, so your system's menu may look different.

Step five is completing the letter. Launch the downloaded file in Microsoft Word and update the highlighted fields with accurate information for this client and this provider. Do not leave any template placeholders behind. A leftover fax number or name from the template is one of the most common mistakes on these letters.

Before it goes out, read the letter one more time. Make sure the request is clear, professional, and contains everything the lienholder needs to process it efficiently. If the billing office has to call us back to ask whose account this is, we have lost time on the case.

This annotated example shows the key fields on a returned verification letter: the name of the medical provider, the name of the client, the last date of treatment, the final lien balance amount, and the date the document was signed. These are exactly the details you will check when a response comes back, so learn where they sit on the page.

Step six is sending the letter to the appropriate entity. That means the right provider, the right billing office, or the collections agency if the account has been sent there. Use the method the entity prefers and keep your proof of sending in the file.

Here is a sample healthcare provider balance verification form. It is clearly marked as not a medical records or bills request, so the provider does not route it to records. It names the facility and the client, the date of loss and dates of service, and asks for total charges, insurance available, whether any insurance has not been billed, the amount already paid, and the payors on the account.

This is a sample ROI form, a release for healthcare information. It authorizes the named facility, here St. Clare Hospital, to release the client's records to the firm, and the boxed field shows the period of treatment it covers. Some providers will not discuss an account without a signed authorization, so this often travels with the request.

This is the bottom of the authorization. Make sure the request is properly signed in compliance with HIPAA. Check the date line, the patient's name, date of birth and the signature. An unsigned or incomplete authorization is a common reason a provider refuses to release information, which delays the balance we need.

Next, save the letter in your CMS or Drive, following the firm's established protocols for naming and location. A saved letter is your proof of what was asked and when, and it lets anyone on the team pick up the file and follow up if you are out.

Here is where the letter goes in this example. Open the Processing Documents folder and use the upload button to add the document. Saving it in the agreed folder means the settlement team always knows where to look for verification requests and responses.

Now update the medical record. Look at all the highlighted parts on this screen: the balance verification requested date, the balance verified checkbox, the BV date and the BV notes, here saying the BV was uploaded in the workup processing folder. Then save. Keeping these fields current is what lets everyone see the status at a glance.

Step seven is documentation. Record every action you took and the pertinent information you acquired along the way: when you sent the request, who you spoke with, and what balance you were given. If it is not documented, the next person on the file has no way of knowing it happened.

Here, the lienholder's record shows a notes field where key instructions are recorded, in this example where reduction requests should be sent. Record all relevant details about the lien: the amount, the lienholder, any associated documentation, and the requests made for the client. This is Filevine, so your screen may differ.

This example shows the Liens field filled in with the verified date, the balance and the last day of treatment, and below it the final lien document saved with a clear name. Make sure all case documents, including lien verifications and payments, are complete and accurate before the case moves on.

Our next section is the Final Lien Ledger, the document that closes the loop on a lien. Once a balance has been verified and any negotiation is done, the ledger is how we confirm that every charge, payment and adjustment has been accounted for before the final payment goes out.

A Final Lien Ledger is a detailed document summarizing every transaction on the lien: charges, credits, payments and adjustments. Its purpose is to make sure every financial piece is accounted for accurately before we close out the lien with a final payment. Think of it as the reconciliation behind the balance figure.

When the ledger arrives, verify it before you save it. Check the name of the client, the name of the medical provider, the last day of treatment, the final lien balance amount, and the date it was signed. A ledger with the wrong client name or the wrong provider should never be filed as final.

Here are the key points a Final Lien Ledger should show. Outstanding charges, meaning the original charges that built the balance. Payments made to the lienholder, with dates and amounts. Adjustments, such as negotiated discounts, documented clearly. And once the lien is fully paid, the balance should show zero dollars, meaning the lien has been satisfied.

The ledger must be free of discrepancies, because it serves as a reference for resolving the case. If something does not reconcile, such as a missing payment or a reduction that was not applied, resolve it before disbursement. Everyone involved should know the final balance, so the process stays transparent and there are no surprises.

Our last section is tracking. Verifying a balance only helps if the whole team can see it. Tracking is how we make sure every client and every provider has a request out, a response in, and a current verified number on file.

Keep your CRM or tracking system updated with each client's balance for each provider. Then store every confirmation document from providers in the CRM, whether it arrived by email, fax or portal. That way the file shows both the current verified number and the proof behind it, and nobody has to hunt through an inbox to find it.

This example shows why tracking matters. Northwest Ambulance shows a zero balance because the account was sent to collections. Audit and Adjustment Company is now collecting for that ambulance bill, with a balance of one thousand two hundred twenty-three dollars and twenty-one cents. When an account moves to collections, the balance follows it, so update the tracker with the new holder.

To find the collections agency in the system, search for it by name. Here the search for audit and adjustment returns the matching accounts, with phone, email and billing address. That gives you the contact details to send the verification request to the right party.

Here is the Processing Documents folder inside the Settlement Workup, where ledgers and lien documents are stored, for example a PIP ledger and subrogation ledgers. Storing confirmations here, with clear names, is how the team finds the right document at settlement time.

After you upload, look for the success message confirming the file uploaded successfully, and check that the document now appears in the Processing Documents list. Do not assume an upload worked; confirm it on screen before you move on, then note it in the tracker.

Here is the same upload screen again, so check it for yourself. Find the green success banner at the top, then confirm that the progress bar reads 100% complete and that the new file now appears in the Processing Documents list. Only after you have seen both should you treat the upload as done and record it in your tracker.

Update the Balance Verification Tracker so we can confirm requests were sent for every client, not just the ones we remembered. Keep your notes precise and accurate. The next person reading them needs to know what was sent, to whom, and what came back, especially when a provider's balance changes during the client's case.

One more habit: keep your own separate tracker as a backup, just in case. Systems go down and shared files get changed. A personal backup means you can still see where every request stands and follow up without losing track.

Here is an example of a Balance Verification Tracker in Excel. Each row is a provider for a client, with contact details, request dates and status columns, and highlighting to show what has been sent or verified. Your tracker may be laid out differently, but it should let you see every request at a glance.

This is another tracker layout, a client tracker with one block per client, listing the providers, contact details, balances and detailed remarks for each. Whatever format you use, the remarks should say what was sent, when, to whom, and what came back.
